slides.title: Chain your ideas
slides.body: Compound & Complex Sentences
slides.notes: The chain links are a metaphor: linking words connect short ideas into one strong sentence. Ask: What happens when we link two ideas together?

slides.title: Why is this lesson important?
slides.body:
• Longer, connected sentences make your writing flow.
  • Examiners reward paragraphs that link ideas clearly.
  • These three patterns will level up every essay you write.

slides.title: Two short sentences
slides.body:
The film was long. The story was rich.

How can we join them?

Opinion — Reason — Evidence
slides.notes: Elicit: and, but, so, because, a semicolon. The O-R-E line anchors the final writing task. CCQ: What changes when we join the ideas?

slides.title: Two short sentences
slides.body: The rain stopped. We went for a walk.

slides.title: One sentence. One meaning.
slides.body: When the rain stopped, we went for a walk.
slides.notes: The adverb clause 'when the rain stopped' adds TIME. CCQ: Which idea is the main idea? Which idea is extra?

slides.title: Adverb Clauses: What do they mean?
slides.body:
becausereason
althoughcontrast
when / whiletime
unlessif not
ifcondition
slides.notes: No clickthroughs. Read each word aloud, then give one spoken example per word. The Use task needs because, although, while, unless, when.

slides.title: Form: two sentences
slides.body: The rain stopped. We went for a walk.

slides.title: Form: clause first
slides.body: When the rain stopped, we went for a walk.
slides.notes: Clause first: adverb clause + comma + main clause.

slides.title: Form: clause last
slides.body: We went for a walk when the rain stopped.
slides.notes: Clause last: main clause + adverb clause, no comma.

slides.title: Try it: Join with although
slides.body: The weather was cold. We went swimming.

slides.title: Try it: although
slides.body: Although the weather was cold, we went swimming.
slides.notes: Demo uses isolated content, not the worksheet. CCQ: Why do we need a comma here?

slides.title: Two short sentences
slides.body: The film was long. The story was rich.

slides.title: One sentence. No connector.
slides.body: The film was long; the story was rich.
slides.notes: The semicolon joins two complete ideas with NO connector. Both sides could stand alone. CCQ: Could we use a full stop instead?

slides.title: Form: two ideas
slides.body: Complete idea. Complete idea.

slides.title: Form: idea ; idea
slides.body: Complete idea; complete idea.
slides.notes: Both sides must be complete sentences. The semicolon replaces the full stop.

slides.title: Try it: Join with a semicolon
slides.body: The pool was closed. We swam in the sea.

slides.title: Try it: semicolon
slides.body: The pool was closed; we swam in the sea.
slides.notes: Demo uses isolated content, not the worksheet.

slides.title: Two short sentences
slides.body: The shop was closed. We went home.

slides.title: One sentence. Result.
slides.body: The shop was closed; therefore, we went home.
slides.notes: therefore = result. The adverb shows HOW the ideas connect. CCQ: What word tells us the result?

slides.title: Conjunctive Adverbs: What do they mean?
slides.body:
howevercontrast
thereforeresult
moreoveraddition
otherwisealternative
meanwhileat the same time
slides.notes: No clickthroughs. Read each word aloud with one spoken example. These are the six Part A words.

slides.title: Form: two ideas
slides.body: Complete idea. Complete idea.

slides.title: Form: ; adverb ,
slides.body: Complete idea; adverb, complete idea.
slides.notes: KEY RULE: semicolon BEFORE the adverb, comma AFTER it. No capital letter after the semicolon.

slides.title: Try it: Join with however
slides.body: The restaurant was full. We found a table.

slides.title: Try it: however
slides.body: The restaurant was full; however, we found a table.
slides.notes: Demo uses isolated content, not the worksheet.

slides.title: Choose the connector
slides.body:
Choose the best word for each gap.
Use each word once.
slides.notes: Students work on paper. The word bank: however, therefore, moreover, otherwise, meanwhile, although. Remind: adverbs come after ; and before ,; although takes a comma, not a semicolon.

slides.title: Answers: Part A
slides.body:
1He missed the deadline; therefore, he lost the contract.
2I will start the dinner; meanwhile, you can set the table.
3You must book early; otherwise, all the rooms will be taken.
4Although the economy improved, unemployment stayed high.
5The hotel was full; however, we found another place to stay.
6She is a great writer; moreover, her novel won a prize.

slides.title: Rewrite the pairs
slides.body:
Rewrite each pair as one sentence.
Use the joining method in brackets.
slides.notes: Students work on paper. 10 items. Point to the pattern slides if they get stuck.

slides.title: Answers: Part B (1-5)
slides.body:
1The plan was risky; however, it worked well.
2The first half of the film was slow; the second half was thrilling.
3Although the team trained hard, they lost the final.
4Unless you arrive early, you will not get a seat.
5The evidence was clear; therefore, the jury agreed quickly.

slides.title: Answers: Part B (6-10)
slides.body:
6I prepared the questions; meanwhile, my colleague booked the room.
7We must leave now; otherwise, we will miss the last train.
8While I cooked dinner, my brother set the table.
9When the storm ended, everyone came out of their houses.
10The cafe was packed; every table was taken.

slides.title: Write a paragraph
slides.body:
90–120 words. Give your opinion.

Use 2 compound and 2 complex sentences.

One sentence needs ; adverb ,.

Opinion — Reason — Evidence
slides.notes: 10-minute timed writing. Topics: schools should require uniforms, or students choose their own clothes. Requirements: 2 compound sentences (one with a semicolon or conjunctive adverb), 2 complex sentences with adverb clauses, a comma before and, but, so, or.

slides.title: Chain your ideas
slides.body:
Adverb clauseWhen the rain stopped, we went for a walk.
SemicolonThe film was long; the story was rich.
; adverb ,The shop was closed; therefore, we went home.
slides.notes: Read the three patterns aloud. These are the same sentences the class saw in the demos.
